historical_record.description: The three-story-over-basement wood-frame flats building whose north wall carries the mural went up around 1905, in an Edwardian manner.
The San Francisco Arts Commission approached Oakland muralist Daniel Galvez to paint a mural here, funded through its Murals and Billboards community outreach program for the Mission District.
The Carnaval mural, about 75 feet long and 24 feet high, was painted on the building's north wall by lead artist Daniel Galvez with Dan Fontes, Jaime Morgan, Jan Shields and Keith Sklar.

The mural's dancers and drummers were taken from photographs of the 1979 Carnaval parade by photojournalist Lou Dematteis, the festival's first official photographer; it took six months to paint in a photo-realist style, with trompe l'oeil Victorian detail and a plank cutout of a dancer's arm reaching across a light well.

The mural pictures 24th Street landmarks of the day, among them Galería de la Raza, the Discolandia record store, the restaurant Guadalajara de Noche, the York Theater and the Mission Cultural Center.
The 1983 Carnaval parade and festival used the new mural in its program designs and posters.
An Eastern Neighborhoods Mission survey recorded the building and found it individually eligible for the California Register; the mural itself was not evaluated.

A Carnaval Mural Restoration Project formed by the muralist, the photographer and former Carnaval SF media coordinator Mauricio Aviles raised money for the faded mural, including a $50,000 Community Challenge Grant.
Restored by Daniel Galvez with a team of artists and volunteers, the mural was rededicated with a celebration that included the city's poet laureate, Alejandro Murguía.
The Board of Supervisors voted to start the process of making the Carnaval Mural a city landmark.
The Historic Preservation Commission recommended the Carnaval Mural for landmark designation after a public hearing.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 313, Carnaval Mural.
